la:verb:arcesso.gloss: to send for, call, invite, summon, fetch
senses: to send for, call, invite, summon, fetch
to summon or arraign someone before a court of justice; accuse, inform against
la:verb:arcesso.html:
arcesso (and accerso), īvi, ītum, 3, v. a. (
inf. arcessire and arcessiri, like lacessiri instead of lacessi, freq. and in the best class. writers, though the MSS. and editt. vary very much; cf. Struve, p. 198.—The form accerso, used freq. by Sall., has been unjustly repudiated; cf. Doed. Syn. III. p. 281 sq.; Kritz ad , and the grammarians cited by both; Dietsch,; Rib. prol. in ) [causat. from accedo; cf. incesso from incedo; ar = ad].
Lit., to cause any one to come, to call, send for, invite, summon, fetch (while accio designates merely the calling, without indicating the coming of the person called, Doed. Syn. III. p. 283).
In gen.: aliquem ad aliquem,: Blepharonem arcessat, qui nobiscum prandeat,: quaeso, hominem ut jubeas arcessi,; so ; ; ; so, arcessiturus,; : arcessitum,: jussit me ad se accersier, Bentl., where Fleck. reads arcessier: obstetricem arcesse,; so ; and : cum ab aratro arcessebantur, qui consules fierent,: sacra ab exteris nationibus ascita atque arcessita,; so : ejus librum arcessivi,: ex continenti alios (fabros) accersi jubet, Dinter: Gabinium accersit,; so ; 60, 4: cunctos senatorii ordinis accersiri jubet,; so : Agrippam ad se arcessi jussit,: Pisonem arcessi jubet,: placere patrem arcessiri,: aliquem ab Epidauro Romam arcessendum,: Ityn huc arcessite,; so ; : sin melius quid (sc. vini) habes, arcesse,order it, let it be brought,—Trop.: Illic homo a me sibi malam rem arcessit jumento suo, prov.,this man brings misfortunes upon his own head,: quies molli strato arcessita,; so, somnum medicamentis,: gloriam ex periculo, al.—
Esp. in judic. lang., to summon, arraign one, before a court of justice; hence, in gen., to accuse, inform against; constr. aliquem alicujus rei: ut hunc hoc judicio arcesseret,; so : ne quem umquam innocentem judicio capitis arcessas,to accuse of a capital crime,: aliquem capitis,: pecuniae captae,: majestatis,: tumultus hostilis,: veneni crimine,; also absol.: arcessiri statim ac mori jussus est,.—Trop.: inscitiae, Nigid. ap . —
Transf. to mental objects, to bring, fetch, seek, or derive a subject, thought, quality, etc.: a capite quod velimus,; so : translationes orationi splendoris aliquid arcessunt,: ex medio res arcessere,: longe arcessere fabulas coepi,to fetch from far,.—Hence, arcessitus (in opp. to that which comes of itself, and is therefore natural), far-fetched, forced, unnatural (syn. durus): cavendum est, ne arcessitum dictum putetur,that an expression may not appear forced, far-fetched,: frigidi et arcessiti joci,: in Lysiā nihil est inane, nihil arcessitum,; cf. ; ;

la:noun:architectus.html:
archĭtectus, i, m., = ἀρχιτέκτων (the usual form, while † archĭtecton, ŏnis, is rare).
Form architectus.
A master-builder, architect: fabri architectique,: Philo architectus,; so ; ; ; ; ; : ut sapiens architectus, al.—
Trop., an inventor, deviser, contriver, author, maker: bene factis Juppiter architectus, ( = auctor atque opifex, Lambin.): inventor veritatis et quasi architectus beatae vitae Epicurus, (cf. : architectari voluptates): princeps atque architectus sceleris,: Stoici architecti paene verborum,.—Hence, archĭtecta, ae, f., a female architect: natura architecta vis,.—
Form architecton.
A master-builder, architect, etc.: nam sibi laudavisse hasce ait architectonem, Nescio quem, esse aedificatas has sane bene,; ; —
Trop., a master in cunning, a crafty man: me quoque dolis jam superat architectonem,.

la:adj:arcanus.html:
arcānus, a, um, adj.
v. arceo
, orig.,
shut up, closed; hence, trop.,
That keeps a secret, trusty: dixisti arcano satis,: petiit, ut aliquem ex arcanis mitteret,.— Hence, poet., of the night: omina arcanā nocte petita, in silent night, or night that keeps secrets, ; .—
Hidden, concealed, secret, private (class., although very rare in Cic.): at quīcum joca, seria, ut dicitur, quīcum arcana, quīcum occulta omnia,: consilia,; so : secretae et arcanae opes,: fontis arcani aqua,: libidines,: littera celatos arcana fatebitur ignes,: sensus,— Esp., in the lang. of religion, of things sacred and incommunicable: ARCANA VRBIS PRAESIDIA,: audivit arcana verba, quae non licet homini loqui, ; and of secret, mysterious usages: sacra,: arcana cum fiunt sacra,; so ; ; ; and by poet. license transf. to the deity presiding over such mysteries: qui Cereris sacrum Volgavit arcanae,.—Hence, subst.: arcānum, i, n., a secret.
In gen.: nox arcanis fidissima,: arcani Fides prodiga,: si quid umquam arcani sanctive ad silendum in curiā fuerit,: arcana regum,: revelare arcana,: denudare arcana amici,.—
Spec., a sacred secret, a mystery: fatorum arcana,; so : Pythagorae arcana,; cf.: Jovis arcana,the secret decrees of,: deorum arcanum proferre,: arcana quaedam, secret rites (of the diviners), : violabunt arcanum meum,my secret place, sanctuary, et saep.—Adv.: arcā-nō (cf. Charis. pp. 173 and 179 P.), in secret, privately: arcano tibi ego hoc dico,: hunc (librum) lege arcano convivis tuis, (cf. Charis. l. c.): arcano cum paucis familiaribus suis colloquitur,.— * Comp.: arcanius judicare aliquid de aliquā re,fin.—Sup. not used.

la:verb:arceo.gloss: to keep off, keep away, ward off, reject, repel
senses: to keep off, keep away, ward off, reject, repel
to keep away, take off, move away, alienate
la:verb:arceo.html:
arcĕo, cui, ctum (arcitum, acc. to P.) [cf. ἀρκέω = to keep off, to suffice; ἄρκιος = sufficient, safe; arx = a stronghold; arca = a strong-box, chest; ἀλαλκεῖν = to keep off; ἀλκή = defence, strength. Curt.].
To shut up, to enclose.
Lit.: arcere est continere, Paul. ex Müll.: alvus arcet et continet quod recipit,: orbis caelestis arcens et continens ceteros, : nos flumina arcemus, dirigimus, avertimus,: hos quidem ut famulos vinclis prope ac custodiā arceamus,shut in, confine, (cf. Doed. Syn. II. p. 426).—
Trop.: videbam audaciam tam immanem non posse arceri otii finibus,.—Also, to keep in order: arcendae familiae gratiā, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. noverca, p. 175 Müll.—
To keep or hold off, to prevent from approaching, to keep at a distance: arcere prohibere est, Paul. ex Müll.; constr. absol. aliquem, with ab, the simple abl., poet. also with dat.
Absol. aliquem: ille tenet et scit ut hostium copiae, tu ut aquae pluviae arceantur,; so, aquam pluviam, aquas pluvias arcere,, and : platanus solem arcet,: somnos ducere et arcere,: Odi profanum vulgus et arceo,.— With an abstr. object: transitum hostis,to arrest, hinder,.—Poet. and in postAug. prose, with inf. as object, to hinder, prevent: quae (dicta) clamor ad aures Arcuit ire meas,: plagamque sedere Cedendo arcebat,; so ; ; ; ; ; .— And without object: arcuit Omnipotens,.—
With ab: tu, Juppiter, hunc a tuis aris ceterisque templis arcebis,: homines ab injuriā, etc.,: haec aetas a libidinibus arcenda est,: homines ab improbitate,: famulas a limine templi,: aliquem ab amplexu,: ignavum, fucos, pecus a praesepibus arcent,.—
With the simple abl. (not with persons): primordia genitali concilio arceri tempore iniquo,: illum ut hostem arcuit Galliā,: te dominus illis sedibus arcebit,fin.; so : Virginiam matronae sacris arcuerant,: aliquem aditu,; so ; : aquā atque igni arcebatur,; so (cf. aqua, I. B. 3.) al.: arceor aris,: patriis penatibus, al.: aliquem funesto veterno,i. e. to protect, guard,: classes aquilonibus, et saep.—
With dat., to keep off something from: oestrum pecori, (cf.: Solstitium pecori defendite,: mortem fratri depulit,; and the Gr. ἀμύνειν νηυσὶ θοῇσι πῦρ, Hom. Il. 9, 435; 9, 347; v. also Rudd. II. p. 150).

la:noun:arcus.html:
arcus, ūs, m. (the orthography, arquus (cf. arquatus), is freq. in MSS., like quum for cum, quur for cur, etc.; cf. Thus P. upon , reads arcuis; P. arci; and , upon , arqui; but the distinction which the latter gram. points out (arcus suspensus fornix appellatur; arquus non nisi qui in caelo apparet, quam Irim poëtae dixerunt) does not seem to be well founded.—
Abl. plur. never found; acc. to the gram., Don. p. 1751,, , Rhem. Palaem. p. 1371 P. al., it was arcubus; so Esdr. 4, 13; cf. Rudd. I. p. 104, n. 48.—Gen. sing. arqui, Lachm., and B. and K.—Dat. arcu, .—Nom. plur. ARCVVS, Corp. Inscr. V. 85; Inscr. Henz. 5313: arci, Varr. ap. .—Acc. ARCOS, Corp. Inscr. II. 3420.—Fem., Enn. ap. P.; cf. P.; and , says that Catull. and others used it as fem.; v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 679) [cf. Sanscr. arālas = bent, the bent arm, aratnis = Gr. ὠλένη; Lat. ulna; Germ. Elbogen; Engl. elbow. Curt.], prop., something bent; hence,
A bow (syn. cornu).
For shooting: intendit crinitus Apollo Arcum auratum, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 54 Müll.): arcus intentus in aliquem,: haec cernens arcum intendebat Apollo Desuper,; ; so ; : arcum tendere,; : adductus,: remissus,: arcum dirigere in aliquem,: quom arcum et pharetram mi et sagittas sumpsero,; so, arcum suscitare, et saep. —
The rainbow (fully: pluvius arcus, v.infra, II.), Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 393 Vahl.): Tum color in nigris existit nubibus arqui, * Lachm.: arcus ipse ex nubibus efficitur quodam modo coloratis,: ceu nubibus arcus Mille jacit varios adverso sole colores, Rib.; so ; ; : pluvius describitur arcus,; ; ; ; and 6: arcum meum ponam in nubibus, sqq. (in ; , iris, q. v.) al.—
A bow or arch in building, a vault, arch, triumphal arch, etc.: efficiens humilem lapidum compagibus arcum,; ; ; : marmoreus arcus,; so ; ; cf. Schwarz.—
Transf.
Poet. or in post-Aug. prose, any thing arched or curved like a bow; of the breaking of waves: niger arcus aquarum,.—Of the windings of a serpent: immensos saltu sinuatur in arcus,.—Of a curve in flight: dea se paribus per cælum sustulit alis Ingentemque fugā secuit sub nubibus arcum,.—Of the curving or bendings of a bay: sinus curvos falcatus in arcus, (cf.: inque sinus scindit sese unda reductos,).— Of a harbor: Portus ab Euroo fluctu curvatus in arcum,.—Of boughs of trees, et saep.—Of the back of a chair, .—
The mathematical arc, ; .—Hence, of the five parallel circles of the globe which bound the zones (or perhaps rather, the zones themselves): via quinque per arcus,.

la:noun:arcturus.html:
arctūrus, i, m., = ἀρκτοῦρος.
As a star.
The brightest star in Bootes,, whose rising and setting was supposed to portend tempestuous weather (): stella micans radiis, Arcturus,; (as a transl. of Arat. 95); cf. ; ; ; ; ; ib. Amos, 5, 8; introduced in as Prologus.—Transf.
The whole constellation (syn.: Bootes, Arctophylax), Voss.—
The rising of Arcturus, .—
A plant, v. arction.

arca, ae, f.
arceo: arca et arx quasi res secretae, a quibus omnes arceantur,; v. arceo
,
a place for keeping any thing, a chest, box.
Lit.
In gen.: arca vestiaria,: ex illā oleā arcam esse factam eoque

conditas sortes, ; : arca ingens variorum venenorum plena,—Very freq.,

Esp.,
A box for money, a safe, a coffer, and particularly of the rich, and loculi was their purse, porte-monnaie, while sacculus was the pouch of the poor, ; ; cf. ; Ruperti, and ; Müll.: populus me sibilat: at mihi plaudo Ipse domi, simul ac nummos contemplor in arcā,.—Hence, meton., like our purse, for the money in it: arcae nostrae confidito,rely upon my purse,; ; ; ; ; ; ; — Hence, ex arcā absolvere aliquem, to pay in cash upon the spot (opp. de mensae scripturā absolvere), Don.; cf. Don., and arcarius.—And of public money, state treasure, revenues (late Lat.): frumentaria,: vinaria,—
A coffin (cf. Smith, Dict. Antiq.), ; cf. ; : cadavera Conservus vili portanda locabat in arcā,; ; ; ; .—
Transf. Of any thing in the form of a box or chest.
Noah's ark (eccl. Lat.), sqq.; ; —
In Jewish antiq., the Ark of the Covenant (eccl. Lat.): arca foederis,: arca foederis Domini,: arca testimonii,: arca testamenti,: arca testamenti Dei,: arca Domini,: arca Dei,; and absol.: arca,; .—
A small, close prison, a cell: (Servi) in arcas coniciuntur, ne quis cum iis colloqui possit,; cf. Müll. —
In mechanics, the water-box of a hydraulic machine, .—
A watercistern, a reservoir, .—
A quadrangular landmark; cf. Scriptt. Agrim. pp. 119, 222, 223, 271 Goes.

la:other:Arctos.html:
arctŏs (nom. arctos, ; acc. arcton, ; ; ; :
arctum, (in verse); nom. plur. arctoe (as in Ter. Adelphoe for Adelphi), , and Arat. Phaen. 441 B. and K.; C. and 63), i, f. (cf. Rudd. I. p. 27; Neue, Formenl. I. pp. 650 sq.; 129; 131), = ἄρκτος.
Lit., the Great and the Lesser Bear (Ursa Major et Minor; syn.: ursa, plaustrum, Septentrio), a double constellation (hence, geminae,; ) in the vicinity of the north pole; cf. Among the poets, on account of its place in the north, gelidae arcti, ; ; cf. ; and since it never sets to our hemisphere, immunis aequoris,: aequoris expers,: metuens aequore tingui, (an imitation of the Homeric: ἄμμορος λοετρῶν Ὠκεανοῖο, Il. 18, 489; Od. 5, 275; cf. also Arat. Phaen. 48: Ἄρκτοι κυανέου πεφυλαγμέναι Ὠκεανοῖο).—
Metaph.
The north pole, .—
The night (cf. luna), .—
The people dwelling in the north, : post domitas Arctos,; .—
The north wind, .

la:noun:Arcas.html:
Arcăs, ădis, m., = Ἀρκάς.
Son of Jupiter and Callisto, the progenitor of the Arcadians, after his death placed as a constellation (Arctophylax) in heaven, ; ; ; ; , and Astr. 2, 4 (cf. Apollod. 3, 8, 2).—
An Arcadian; plur.Arcădĕs, um, m. (acc. Gr. Arcadăs, ), = Ἀρκάδες, the Arcadians.
As the most ancient men, ; —
As skilled in pastoral music: Tamen cantabitis, Arcades, inquit, Montibus haec vestris; soli cantare periti, Arcades,: Arcades ambo, Et cantare pares et respondere parati, (cf. sq.; Theocr. 22, 157; Polyb. 4, 20).—Hence, Arcas,
Κατʼ ἐξοχήν.
Mercury, who was said to have been born on the Arcadian mountain Cyllene (cf. 1. Arcadia, B.), ; ; .—
Parthenopœus, the son of Atalanta from Arcadia, ; .—
Tyrannus, i. e. Lycaon, grandfather of Arcas (a poet. prolepsis), .—
Bipennifer, i. e. Ancœus, .—
Adj., = Arcadius, Arcadian, ; ; ; ; .
